items.q: The ultrafiltration (UF) coefficient used in the book's worked GFR calculation is:
items.exp: GFR = [(60 − 18) − (32 − 0)] × 12.5 ml/min/mmHg; the 10 mmHg net pressure is multiplied by this coefficient, not by 1.25 or 25. (Book p734)

items.q: In the expansion of the equation, the bracketed net hydrostatic pressure difference (glomerular capillary HP − Bowman's space HP) works out to:
items.exp: (60 − 18) = 42 mmHg is the net hydrostatic term; the 10 mmHg net filtration pressure appears only after the 32 mmHg oncotic term is subtracted. (Book p734)

items.q: All of these pressures appear in the boxed net filtration pressure equation on this page EXCEPT:
items.exp: The box reads: net filtration pressure (10) = glomerular hydrostatic (60) − Bowman's capsule (18) − glomerular oncotic (32). The capsular oncotic pressure appears only in the written expansion above, where it is taken as zero. (Book p734)

items.q: In the capillary–capsule diagram, the arrow drawn for Bowman's capsule pressure points back towards the glomerular capillary, i.e. it opposes filtration.
opts: True — it is subtracted in the calculation for exactly that reason
False — capsular pressure is shown favouring filtration
True — capsular pressure is one of the two forces that raise GFR
False — the diagram labels capsular pressure without any arrow
items.exp: The 60 mmHg hydrostatic and 32 mmHg colloid osmotic arrows are drawn outwards from the capillary, while the 18 mmHg Bowman's capsule pressure arrow points back at it; hydrostatic favours and the other two oppose filtration. (Book p734)

items.q: The definition of GFR printed on this page refers to filtration by:
opts: All the nephrons in both kidneys in one minute
The nephrons of one kidney in one minute
All nephrons in both kidneys over 24 hours
Only those glomeruli filtering at the time of measurement
items.exp: Definition: amount of urine filtered by all the nephrons in both kidneys in one minute — a per-minute, both-kidney figure. (Book p734)
